levels.title: Level 1 — Listener
levels.sub: What a signal is, how to tune one, and what you're allowed to do with it.

modules.title: Radio waves, frequency & wavelength
body: A radio signal is an electromagnetic wave. Its frequency is how many times per second it oscillates (1 kHz = 1,000/s, 1 MHz = 1,000,000/s). Its wavelength is how far it travels during one oscillation.
Wavelength in metres ≈ 300 / frequency in MHz. CHU at 7.85 MHz has a ~38 m wavelength; airband at 121.5 MHz is ~2.5 m; ADS-B at 1090 MHz is ~27 cm.

Engineers split the spectrum into bands: LF (30–300 kHz), MF (0.3–3 MHz, AM radio), HF (3–30 MHz, "shortwave" — bounces around the world), VHF (30–300 MHz, FM radio and airband — line-of-sight) and UHF (300 MHz–3 GHz).
modules.key: Lower frequency → longer wave → travels further around the Earth. Higher frequency → shorter wave → mostly line-of-sight.

quiz.q: What is the approximate wavelength of a 100 MHz FM station?

modules.title: Modulation: AM, FM, SSB and CW
body: A plain carrier wave carries no information. Modulation changes it to carry sound or data.

AM varies the strength — used by AM broadcast, shortwave broadcast and aviation VHF (two stations transmitting at once are both still heard, which matters for safety). FM varies the frequency — clean audio for FM radio, marine VHF and NOAA Weatheradio.

SSB (single sideband, USB/LSB) removes the carrier and one half of an AM signal to save power — used for HF voice by hams, oceanic aircraft and ships. If SSB sounds like Donald Duck, you're slightly mistuned. CW is Morse code: the carrier simply switched on and off.
modules.key: Pick the right mode or you hear noise: AM for airband & broadcast, USB/LSB for HF voice, FM for VHF voice.

quiz.q: Which mode is used for civil aviation voice on VHF?
quiz.why: Aviation VHF uses AM so overlapping transmissions are both audible.

modules.title: Web SDRs and reading a waterfall
body: A software-defined radio (SDR) digitises a whole slice of spectrum and lets software do the tuning. KiwiSDR, WebSDR and OpenWebRX owners share theirs over the internet — that's what the Radio tab lists.

The waterfall is the scrolling picture: horizontal = frequency, vertical = time, brightness = signal strength. Steady vertical lines are carriers; dotted lines are Morse; fuzzy columns ~3 kHz wide are SSB voice; wide stripes are broadcasts.
Each receiver has a limited number of user slots. Be polite: close the tab when done, respect time limits.
modules.key: Click on a signal in the waterfall to tune it, then adjust mode and filter width until it sounds clear.

quiz.q: On a waterfall, the vertical axis shows…
quiz.why: Frequency runs left–right, time scrolls top-down, brightness is strength.

modules.title: Your first catch: time signals
body: Time stations broadcast continuously, so they're the perfect first target. CHU in Ottawa announces the time in English and French on 3.330, 7.850 and 14.670 MHz. WWV (Colorado) and WWVH (Hawaii) share 2.5/5/10/15/20 MHz.
Whether you can hear them from a given receiver tells you about propagation — which frequencies are "open" between two places right now.
modules.key: If CHU on 7.850 is loud from a European receiver, the 40 m path across the Atlantic is open.

quiz.q: Where is the CHU time station?
quiz.why: CHU is run by the National Research Council in Ottawa.

modules.title: What's legal in Canada
body: Under the Radiocommunication Act, listening to the radio spectrum is generally allowed. Broadcasts, amateur radio, time and weather stations are meant for everyone.

What is restricted: divulging or using a private radiocommunication you happen to hear (s.9(2)) — e.g. posting a ship-to-ship call or an airline's datalink message — and decoding encrypted signals or subscription services (s.9(1)(c)). Accessing cameras or devices you're not authorised to use is a Criminal Code offence even with no password.
This app only surfaces receivers, cameras and feeds that their owners published on purpose.
modules.key: Listen and learn freely; don't share or act on private traffic, and never bypass encryption or log-ins.

quiz.q: You hear a ship-to-ship conversation on a public SDR. What is OK?
opts: Use the info to win a bid
quiz.why: Listening is fine; divulging or using private comms is not.

levels.title: Level 2 — Operator
levels.sub: Why signals go where they go, and the services you can follow.

modules.title: Propagation: why HF changes with the clock
body: HF signals bend off the ionosphere, layers of charged gas 60–400 km up, created by sunlight. By day the low D-layer absorbs lower HF frequencies; at night it vanishes and the F-layer still reflects lower frequencies — so low bands open up after dark, high bands by day.

The MUF (maximum usable frequency) is the highest frequency that still reflects on a given path. That's why VOLMET uses 3.485 MHz at night and 13.282 MHz by day, and why AM broadcast travels 1000+ km at night.
Solar activity matters too: more sunspots → higher MUF → 10–15 m bands come alive.
modules.key: Night: go lower (2–8 MHz). Day: go higher (10–20 MHz).

quiz.q: After sunset, which frequency is more likely to reach across the Atlantic?
quiz.why: Lower HF frequencies propagate best at night.

modules.title: Following aircraft: VHF, HF oceanic and ADS-B
body: Over land, pilots talk to controllers on VHF AM (118–137 MHz). It's line-of-sight, so you need a receiver within ~100–200 km of the aircraft.
Over the North Atlantic there is no VHF coverage, so aircraft call Gander and Shanwick on HF USB (NAT frequency families A/B/C) to give position reports.

ADS-B: aircraft broadcast GPS position, altitude and callsign on 1090 MHz about twice a second, unencrypted, by design. Volunteers feed it to aggregators like adsb.fi — that's the Flights tab. Squawk codes 7500/7600/7700 mean hijack / radio failure / emergency.
modules.key: Match a flight in the Flights tab with a Gander HF position report — that's how oceanic tracking used to work.

quiz.q: What frequency do aircraft use for ADS-B?

modules.title: Amateur radio, call signs & beacons
body: Licensed hams talk worldwide, experiment and help in emergencies. In Canada you need the ISED Basic qualification to transmit — listening needs no licence.
Call signs encode location: VY2 is Prince Edward Island, VE1 Nova Scotia, VE9 New Brunswick, VO1 Newfoundland. US calls start with K, N, W or A.
The 18 NCDXF beacons take turns sending their call sign in Morse on 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz every 10 s — a free propagation map.
modules.key: Hear a VY2 or VE1 on 40 m in the evening? That's a local station via near-vertical skywave.

quiz.q: Which call-sign prefix belongs to Prince Edward Island?

modules.title: Marine & weather services
body: Ships use VHF FM channel 16 (156.8 MHz) for distress and calling, and HF 2182/4125/6215/8291 kHz for safety. The Canadian Coast Guard broadcasts continuous marine weather on VHF.
Weatherfax: Halifax (CFH) and Boston (NMF) send weather charts as audio tones on HF. Tune 1.9 kHz below the published frequency in USB and a decoder such as fldigi draws the chart.
NOAA / Environment Canada Weatheradio uses seven channels between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz.
modules.key: Data signals sound like warbles or buzzes — the information is in the pattern, decoded by software.

quiz.q: Which VHF channel is the marine distress & calling channel?

modules.title: Digital modes: FT8, APRS, NAVTEX, ACARS
body: Many signals are data. FT8 (14.074 MHz) lets hams make contacts with signals too weak to hear; APRS (144.390 MHz in North America) carries positions and weather as 1200-baud packets; NAVTEX (518 kHz) sends maritime safety text.
ACARS (131.550 MHz and others) carries airline text messages. It's fine to identify the signal; treat the content as private — don't log or share it.
Public aggregators (PSK Reporter, aprs.fi) show what volunteer receivers decode in real time.
modules.key: Identify a signal by its sound + bandwidth + frequency; the Signal ID wiki has audio samples of hundreds of modes.

quiz.q: In North America, APRS is on…
quiz.why: 144.390 MHz in North America; 144.800 MHz in Europe.

levels.title: Level 3 — Engineer
levels.sub: Your own receiver, antennas, decibels and DSP.

modules.title: Your own receiver: the RTL-SDR
body: An RTL-SDR (e.g. RTL-SDR Blog V4, ~$40 CAD) is a TV-tuner chip repurposed as a 500 kHz–1.7 GHz receiver. It streams raw samples to your laptop; software like SDR++ does the rest.
Key settings: sample rate (how much spectrum you see at once — about 2.4 MHz), gain (too high overloads, too low hides weak signals), and direct sampling / upconverter for HF.
rtl_tcp or OpenWebRX can share it over your Wi-Fi, which is what the Local RX tab will connect to.
modules.key: Start with gain around 30–40 dB and lower it if the waterfall fills with false signals.

quiz.q: At 2.4 MS/s, roughly how wide a slice of spectrum can you see?
quiz.why: With IQ (complex) sampling, visible bandwidth ≈ sample rate.

modules.title: Antennas, decibels and noise
body: A half-wave dipole is two wires, total length ≈ 143 / f(MHz) metres. For 1090 MHz that's ~13 cm; for 7 MHz ~20 m. Height and distance from household electronics matter more than almost anything.
Decibels are ratios: +3 dB = double the power, +10 dB = ten times. SNR is how far the signal is above the noise floor — 10 dB SNR is comfortable voice.
Indoors, LED bulbs, chargers and monitors create a "noise floor" that can bury weak HF signals. Outside and away from the house is always better.
modules.key: Improving the antenna beats buying a better radio.

quiz.q: A signal goes up by 3 dB. Its power has…

modules.title: DSP basics: IQ, Nyquist and filters
body: An SDR samples the signal as two streams, I and Q (in-phase and quadrature), letting software tell frequencies above and below the centre apart.
Nyquist: to represent a signal you must sample at least twice its highest frequency (for real samples); otherwise strong signals fold back as phantom aliases.
Demodulators are just maths on those samples: AM = magnitude, FM = rate of phase change, SSB = shift and filter. A narrower filter rejects more noise but can make voice muffled.
modules.key: If a strong signal appears in two places, suspect overload or aliasing before anything else.

tries.label: Experiment with filters on a KiwiSDR

quiz.q: Real (non-IQ) sampling at 48 kHz can faithfully capture audio up to…
quiz.why: Nyquist limit = half the sample rate.

modules.title: Project: become an ADS-B feeder
body: With an RTL-SDR and a 1090 MHz antenna (a 13 cm dipole or a ground-plane), readsb or dump1090 decodes aircraft overhead. Put the antenna high with a clear view of the sky.
Feeding adsb.fi or adsb.lol shares your data publicly and helps coverage around PEI. In return you get stats and the satisfaction of putting dots on the map.
Bonus: a Raspberry Pi can run it 24/7 using a few watts.
modules.key: Line-of-sight is everything: every extra metre of antenna height adds range.

quiz.q: Which antenna length suits 1090 MHz (half-wave dipole)?

modules.title: Project: weather satellite images
body: Russia's Meteor-M satellites transmit LRPT images on ~137.9 / 137.1 MHz. With an RTL-SDR, a V-dipole or QFH antenna and SatDump, you can decode cloud pictures during a ~12 min pass. (NOAA-15/18/19 APT stopped in 2025.)
Use a pass predictor (N2YO, Gpredict) and record when the satellite is above ~20° elevation. The Doppler shift moves the signal a few kHz during the pass.
The ISS occasionally sends SSTV images on 145.800 MHz FM for everyone to decode.
modules.key: Timing beats hardware: be ready before the pass starts.

quiz.q: Which satellites still send weather images near 137 MHz?
quiz.why: NOAA APT retired in 2025; Meteor-M LRPT continues.
